No fabricated number was found among the claims that could be checked; one load-bearing source (Getty lender deck) could not be verified at all.

suspect_claims.claim: L37: "Deals sourced from private individuals' personal media. Three were found." and L11: "the one platform that tried to license a consumer photo archive (Photobucket)"
suspect_claims.problem: Contradicted by an omission. GoPro launched an opt-in AI Training program on 2025-07-30: US subscribers license their cloud-stored personal footage for third-party model training and receive 50% of the licence revenue; 125,000+ hours opted in within about two weeks, 300,000+ hours by 2025-12-11, and GoPro's 10-Q filed 2026-08-10 describes the program (gopro.com/en/us/info/ai-training-program; nasdaq.com press releases of 2025-07-30 and 2025-12; dataconto.com/open-data/sec-filings). This is the closest public precedent to the variant (personal archive plus revenue share, listed company with filings) and the file does not mention GoPro once. Whether GoPro has booked any revenue from it was not found in one search, so the file's 'no revenue disclosed' statement may still hold, but it was reached without looking at the obvious case.

suspect_claims.claim: L32: Freepik at 2 to 4 cents "is the only closed per-image bulk price found"; L33: "Adobe's 2024 per-minute video purchases: [unknown] (the Bloomberg report could not be retrieved)"; L91: base price per item $0.03
suspect_claims.problem: One WebSearch returns the Bloomberg 2024-04-10 report through TechCrunch, PetaPixel, The Register and PYMNTS: Adobe paid about $2.62 per minute on average and up to $7.25 per minute for training video, and 6 to 16 cents per photo for training images. That is a second paid per-image price, two to five times Freepik's, and a per-minute figure the brief asked for. The Q6 base ($0.03), the $12 / $3 per-roll headline and the '3.3 billion licences for $100M' line all rest on Freepik alone; at Adobe's range the base roll grosses $24 to $64. The conclusion (small) survives, the stated magnitude does not.

suspect_claims.claim: L9: "Getty filed a prepackaged Chapter 11 on 2026-10-21 ... Still-image licensing peaked in 2025." and L108 (Q7): "Prices or volumes are falling | ... Getty in Chapter 11 | Supported for stills"
suspect_claims.problem: The filing date is correct (Octus, ABF Journal, Bloomberg Law), but the bankruptcy is used as evidence of falling demand. The CEO's first-day declaration, as summarised by Octus, attributes the filing to 'non-operational events': warrant-holder litigation judgments of more than $200M, $275M of unasserted warrant claims, the failed Shutterstock merger and debt service of about $239M a year. Twelve-month revenue to 2026-06-30 was about $978M with about $307M adjusted EBITDA. Chapter 11 here is a balance-sheet event, not a licensing-demand datum, and should be removed from the Q7 evidence column.

suspect_claims.claim: L9, L30, L59, L108, table rows 5-6: Getty lender deck puts AI data licensing at 2.6% (FY2024), 4.4% (FY2025), 3.4% (LTM Q2 2026) of revenue; derived $24M / $43M / $33M
suspect_claims.problem: Not verifiable. The cited exhibit (sec.gov ...000121390026108700/ea030834301ex99-2.htm) returned 403 here, and two searches (one extended) found no page carrying 2.6%, 4.4% or 3.4%. A tracker that read the same 2026-10-13 8-K exhibit extracted only '~$40MM of revenue recognized on an accelerated basis in Q4 2025'. The surrounding facts check out (8-K with an investor presentation on 2026-10-13; LTM revenue $978M; FY2025 revenue $981.3M), so the numbers are plausible, but three derived dollar figures and the '4.4% to 3.4%' decline rest on a page nobody but the author has seen. A verifiable substitute exists and was not used: Getty's Q2 2026 10-Q shows Other revenue of $5.2M, down 66.7% from $15.7M, on 'fewer higher-value agreements'.

suspect_claims.claim: L89: share licensable base 12.7% = "Kled's realized figure, 200M corpus files / 500,000 contributors = 400 files, / 3,139"; L97: cross-check "400 items x $0.0073 = $2.92, within 3% of the base $3.00"
suspect_claims.problem: The base is not the quantity the brief asked for (share left after excluding identifiable people, minors, screenshots, duplicates). It divides a seller's catalogue size by a claimed head-count that includes banned and inactive accounts, then by a 2023 survey mean from a different population; the corpus is items contributors chose, includes video, and is face-masked rather than face-excluded. The author's own source cuts against it: Kled's founder said in May 2026 that users had uploaded 'over 1 billion assets' (Premium Times), which implies roughly 2,000+ uploads per contributor and about 20% retained, not 400 items per roll. The cross-check is not independent: item count cancels, so it only says one Reddit anecdote ($0.0073) happens to equal $0.03 x the assumed 25% share ($0.0075).

suspect_claims.claim: L9: "Still-image licensing peaked in 2025."; L59: "A catalog can be sold to each large buyer once; the first-wave buyers have it."
suspect_claims.problem: Forecast stated as fact, untagged. Direction is corroborated (Shutterstock DDS nine months down 46%; Getty Other down 66.7% in Q2 2026; Wiley's AI line down 53%), but the headline 91% is one quarter against a +40% comparison quarter, the data offering was down 63% in Q1 and only 11% in Q2, and Shutterstock says recognition 'may vary from quarter-to-quarter based on the delivery timing'. Should read as 'fell in 2026 to date', tagged.

suspect_claims.claim: L47: Kled "Seed of $5.5M announced 2026-03-10; company says total funding is $14M"
suspect_claims.problem: The cited review dates the $5.5M seed to a June 2026 SaaS News report ('bringing their total financing to $10 million'); March 2026 is the separate Business Insider quote ($6.5M at a $150M valuation). No '2026-03-10' appears on the page. Kled's own site banner on 2026-11-25 reads 'Kled Raises $10M in Funding', not $14M. The file notes that figures conflict but picks $14M for both tables.

suspect_claims.claim: L61: "Video: holds better. $1 to $4 per minute in 2025 ... One aggregator puts realized rates for large catalogs near $0.55 per minute in 2026"
suspect_claims.problem: Internally inconsistent: the only 2026 figure offered is 45% to 86% below the 2025 range, which reads as a fall, not as holding. Both ends are search-summary secondary; the 2026 figure is from a broker's marketing page.

suspect_claims.claim: L35: Reddit Other revenue "$140M in FY2025, up 22% ... Growth slowed through 2025."
suspect_claims.problem: Stale as of the file's date. Reddit's Q2 2026 10-Q (filed 2026-07-31) shows Other revenue of $43.3M, up 24% (talika.ai summary of the filing), so growth re-accelerated in 2026. Three 2026 quarters were available and none was used.

suspect_claims.claim: L72 and table row 24: Delete Act "fine of $200 per consumer per day for failing to register"
suspect_claims.problem: Faithful to TrustArc's wording, but TrustArc appears to merge two penalties: the statute's registration penalty is per day, and the per-request-per-day penalty attaches to failing to delete. The numbers table drops the 'as TrustArc describes' hedge and tags it [sourced]. Check against Civ. Code 1798.99.82 before reuse.

Q1, Adobe: per-minute video and per-photo training purchases answered [unknown] because the Bloomberg page would not load; secondary coverage ($2.62 average, up to $7.25 per minute; 6 to 16 cents per photo) is one search away.
Q1, Flickr/SmugMug: a single April 2024 quote; current policy [unknown] with no record of reading Flickr's own terms or AI statement.

Q1, Shutterstock and Getty detail: Shutterstock's Contributor Fund (20% average royalty on data deals, opt-out since 2023) is not cited although Q6 needs a sourced take rate; named buyers (OpenAI, Meta, Google, Amazon, Apple; Getty's 2026-06-22 OpenAI display deal and 2025-10-30 Microsoft agreement) are missing from the deals table; Getty's Q2 2026 Other revenue ($5.2M, down 66.7%) is not used.

Q1, legal drivers: US Copyright Office report and NYT v. OpenAI rest on secondary trackers with conflicting dates; the EU opt-out regime gets one secondary sentence (no Art. 53(1)(c) copyright-policy duty, no Code of Practice).

Q2: Scale AI/Outlier, Public AI, Datacurve and Created by Humans are dismissed after 'one combined search' with no buyers, prices, payouts, funding or status; Mercor is one aggregator number. None has a row in the marketplaces table.

Q2, [unknown] without evidence of trying: Vana funding (the company's own 2024-09 post gives $25M) and any description of data DAOs; Defined.ai funding, volume and 2026 status; Troveo funding; Kled downloads (no app-intelligence estimate tried, and the stated reason, a failed Play lookup, does not apply to an iOS-only app); Wirestock installs and reviews.
Q2, Kled reviews: the brief asks for reviews; the file gives the star rating and count but no content from App Store reviews, and only two Reddit posts.

Q3: no RFP, broker price sheet or buyer statement, reported [unknown] without a search log; 'do labs still buy still images?' is answered only from sellers' behaviour; no 2026 per-image price; Kled's task pay rates (shown 'upfront' in V3 per its own post) were not collected.

Q4: GDPR Art. 6 lawful basis is not addressed (Art. 9 only); CCPA/CPRA 'sale' and 'sharing' definitions, opt-out and sensitive-personal-information limits are not analysed (data-broker registration only); right-of-publicity statutes are not discussed; FTC posture is one URL-less sentence with no 2024-2026 actions; Shutterstock's model-release rule is [unknown] because a page 'did not render', though the rule is in Shutterstock's contributor help pages and its 10-K.

Q5, surveys: answered [unknown] after one search. Adjacent evidence exists and is unused: CNIL's willingness-to-sell survey (n=2,082; about 4% would sell at EUR 1 a month, about 20% at EUR 4.30) and a 2025 arXiv experiment (67% willing to sell social-media data for $0.25 to $1).

Q5, provenance: C2PA and device attestation rest on one vendor blog seen through a search summary; no marketplace's verification documentation was read. Kled's 'Camera-Original Phone Photos (1M photos)' in-app-capture product, on the datasets page the author did read, is a device-capture provenance mechanism and goes unremarked.

Q6: share licensable is not built by exclusion (identifiable people, minors, screenshots, duplicates) as the brief specifies; low and high brackets have no method; price rests on one 2024 stock-library deal; video items in a roll are never priced per minute although the roll figure is 'pictures and videos'; Shutterstock data-licensing margin commentary is [unknown] with no record of checking earnings-call transcripts.

Q7: Streamlytics and Brave are not examined; the synthetic-data question is closed as [unknown] on one vendor quote with no search for lab statements; 'labs avoid consumer-sourced personal data' has no buyer-side evidence and no record of looking for any (procurement terms, dataset cards, lab policies).
verdict_reason: The spine holds: every checkable primary figure (Shutterstock 10-K and 10-Q, Reuters, TechCrunch, Kled, Troveo, Authors Guild, store listings, regulator pages) matched its source and all arithmetic is right. It is not a pass because (1) it misses the closest precedent to the variant (GoPro) and a second paid per-image price (Adobe) while stating that only three individual-sourced deals and one closed per-image price exist; (2) Getty's Chapter 11 is used as demand evidence when the company attributes it to litigation and leverage; (3) the Getty lender-deck percentages cannot be verified; (4) the middle input of the camera-roll chain is not the estimate the brief asked for; (5) about a dozen numbers carry tags with no URL; (6) a long list of [unknown] answers show one search or none.
